subsystems.name: Biological model analysis
subsystems.role: studies a natural material to extract the design rules that make it work.

subsystems.name: Base material synthesis
subsystems.role: produces the building blocks — polymers, ceramics, composites — that will be structured.

subsystems.name: Hierarchical assembly
subsystems.role: builds structure across scales, from nanometres to millimetres, as nature does.

subsystems.name: Surface and interface engineering
subsystems.role: controls how the material interacts with water, light, or living cells.

subsystems.name: Characterisation and testing
subsystems.role: verifies that the synthetic material actually matches the natural one.

buildSteps.title: Select a biological model
buildSteps.detail: Choose a natural material with a property worth copying — the gecko foot for adhesion, nacre for toughness, bone for lightweight strength, or the lotus leaf for self-cleaning.

buildSteps.title: Extract the design principles
buildSteps.detail: Image the natural material at multiple scales and test it mechanically to identify which structural features, from molecular to macroscopic, produce the desired behaviour.

buildSteps.title: Choose synthetic building blocks
buildSteps.detail: Select polymers, ceramics, metals or composites that can replicate those features and are compatible with the intended application, such as being non-toxic for tissue engineering.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate with controlled architecture
buildSteps.detail: Use techniques like 3D printing, self-assembly, freeze casting or lithography to build the material layer by layer, mimicking the natural hierarchy rather than a uniform solid.

buildSteps.title: Engineer the surfaces
buildSteps.detail: Modify chemistry and texture so the material interacts correctly with its environment — repelling water, promoting cell attachment, or bonding reversibly.

buildSteps.title: Assemble into a device or scaffold
buildSteps.detail: Integrate the material into its final form, such as a tissue scaffold with pores for cells to invade, or a structural panel that must bear load.

buildSteps.title: Test against the natural model
buildSteps.detail: Measure stiffness, strength, toughness, adhesion or biocompatibility and compare with the biological original; iterate on structure and processing until the synthetic version performs as intended.

prerequisites.why: you cannot copy a structure you cannot see, and natural materials often hide their key features at the nanoscale.
most methods control either the nano or the macro scale well, but combining both in one part is still difficult.
it predicts which structural changes will improve performance and reduces trial-and-error experiments.
tissue-engineering scaffolds need materials that cells accept and that degrade at the right rate.
lab techniques like two-photon lithography are far too slow and expensive for commercial production.

pathway.milestone: simple biomimetic surfaces reach niche markets
pathway.unlocks: self-cleaning coatings, gecko-inspired adhesives, and shark-skin-like anti-fouling films.

pathway.milestone: multi-scale fabrication matures so complex hierarchical structures can be made reliably
pathway.unlocks: tougher, lighter composites for aerospace and construction, and better medical implants.

pathway.milestone: living cells are routinely combined with synthetic scaffolds
pathway.unlocks: lab-grown tissues for repair and replacement, reducing reliance on donors.

pathway.milestone: cost-effective, large-scale production of biomimetic materials
pathway.unlocks: widespread use of nature-inspired materials in everyday products, buildings and healthcare.
